# Craniosynostosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Hereditary malformations > Craniosynostosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/g40FiT)

---

## Summary

Craniosynostosis (CS) is the premature fusion of one or more <u>cranial sutures</u>. It is caused by a mutation in <u>genes</u> that code for <u>fibroblast</u> growth factor. Most affected <u>infants</u> are asymptomatic; CS is usually recognized based on an abnormal head shape in the first year of life. The shape of the <u>skull</u> is determined by which suture is prematurely fused, of which the <u>sagittal</u> suture (<u>scaphocephaly</u>) is the most commonly affected. When multiple sutures are involved, CS may cause <u>hydrocephalus</u> and/or cerebral constriction. Diagnosis is clinical, with <u>skull</u> <u>x-ray</u> and <u>CT scan</u> helping to assess the extent of fusion. <u>Surgery</u> is recommended in all <u>infants</u> for cosmetic reasons and to treat/prevent intracranial complications.

---

## Pathophysiology

* The <u>skull</u> is composed of 5 separate bones: 2 frontal bones, 2 parietal bones, and the <u>occipital bone</u>

* In a <u>newborn</u>, these bones are separated by patent sutures and <u>fontanelles</u>.

* Function of patent sutures and <u>fontanelles</u>

* Allow compression and/or overlapping of the <u>skull</u> bones during <u>childbirth</u>

* Allow for growth of the <u>brain</u>

* Premature closure of one or more sutures → craniosynostosis

* See the article on <u>skull</u>.

## Clinical features

* Usually asymptomatic

* Recognized as an abnormal head shape within the first year of life





| <u>Skull</u> deformity due to premature fusion | Suture/s involved | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Scaphocephaly/<u>dolichocephaly</u> (<u>sagittal</u> <u>synostosis</u>) | <br>* <u>Sagittal</u> suture<br><br> | <br><br>* Most common type of CS (∼ 45%)<br><br>* Long, narrow <u>skull</u> (boat-shaped)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Anterior plagiocephaly (unilateral coronal <u>synostosis</u>) | <br>* Unilateral coronal suture<br><br> | <br><br>* 2<sup>nd</sup> most common type of CS<br><br>* Laterally twisted/oblique <u>skull</u> and face<br><br><br> |
| <br>Posterior plagiocephaly (unilateral lambdoid <u>synostosis</u>) | <br>* Unilateral lambdoid suture<br><br> | <br><br>* Rare type of CS<br><br>* Twisted/oblique <u>skull</u><br><br>* Occipitoparietal flattening on the affected side<br><br>* Low-set <u>ears</u> on the affected side<br><br><br> |
| Trigonocephaly | <br>* Metopic suture<br><br> | <br><br>* Common type of CS (∼ 25% of cases)<br><br>* Triangular shaped head<br><br>* Prominent occiput and parietal eminences<br><br>* Close-set eyes (<u>hypotelorism</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Brachycephaly | <br>* Bilateral coronal sutures<br><br> | <br>* Short, broad, flattened <u>skull</u><br><br> |
| <br>Oxycephaly (<u>turricephaly</u>) | <br>* Bilateral coronal sutures (if left untreated)<br><br> | <br>* Long <u>skull</u> (increased craniocaudal dimension)<br><br> |
| Cloverleaf skull | <br>* Multiple <u>cranial sutures</u> (esp. the metopic, coronal, and lambdoid sutures)<br><br> | <br><br>* Rare, but most severe type<br><br>* Trilobar <u>skull</u> (prominent forehead and temporal bulging)<br><br>* Often associated with <u>hydrocephalus</u> and <u>elevated intracranial pressure</u><br><br><br> |

## Differential diagnoses

The following conditions show patency of sutures similar to craniosynostosis on <u>skull</u> <u>x-ray</u> or <u>ultrasound</u>:




* Positional plagiocephaly

* <u>Infant torticollis</u>





References:[[10]](/library/KIaUdN)




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.
